You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# NCAA Best Practices Doc: Draft v1 Read-Only Verification

On 2026-10-04 Draft v1 of Baylor Athletics' "Performance Technology Best Practices" guide (repo `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc`, commit `a9dabb0`) was verified read-only against its own `docs/GOAL_PROMPT.md` and `docs/PLAN.md`. The pass ran through Codex with no edits and no commits, applied a 10-point check list, and returned a split verdict: **PASS on checks 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9; FAIL on 3 (SSI crosswalk), 6 (internal consistency), and 8 (factual support)**. All 12 deliverables existed and rendered correctly — a 9-page guide plus five 2-page appendices (A–E).

## Key Points

- **The artifacts were inspected, not regenerated.** PDFs were read with PyMuPDF rather than re-running the build, because `scripts/build_guide.py` drives Word through COM; re-running it would have produced Word-automation side effects during what was meant to be a non-mutating audit.
- **The three failures are all cross-document failures, not formatting ones.** Build artifacts, outline coverage, pending tags, athlete-data hygiene, terminology, and BaylorDoc styling all passed. What failed was agreement between the guide and its appendices, the accuracy of the SSI crosswalk's coverage claims, and whether specific factual assertions had any source pointer at all.
- **Paired athlete-facing and policy documents drifted apart on the same rule.** Guide §4.3's staff access matrix grants Athletic/Applied Performance *flags only* on raw wellness data, while Appendix A's athlete-facing disclosure says Athletic Performance sees wellness check-ins. The documents describe the same access rule and contradict each other.
- **A consent checkbox silently defeats a stated gate.** Appendix A carries a general research checkbox; Guide §4.5 requires IRB approval *plus* study-specific consent. Signing the general box appears to satisfy a requirement it does not satisfy.
- **A gate form with an "N/A" option is not a gate.** Appendix B permits N/A on rows 1–6, which the guide states must all be met — so the contract gate can be bypassed by marking the mandatory rows inapplicable. The fix recorded is an exception path (documented, approved) rather than removing N/A.
- **Crosswalk "Met" statuses overstated coverage in two rows.** F2 claims international-law coverage that the cited passages never address, and Rec 4.3 says a multidisciplinary group *decides* while the guide says it *reviews* — with Appendix E providing no Working Group decision field to support the stronger verb.

## Details

The useful structure of this verification is that every passing check was intrinsic to a single document and every failing check was relational. A pending-tag sweep, a styling check, a terminology check, and an athlete-data hygiene check can each be answered by reading one file. Internal consistency, crosswalk accuracy, and factual support cannot: they require holding two artifacts side by side and asking whether the second is entitled to what it says about the first. This is why a guide can be complete, correctly built, correctly styled, free of placeholder markers, and still be unsafe to publish — the defects live in the seams. The specific seams here were guide-to-appendix (access matrix vs. disclosure; mandatory rows vs. N/A column), guide-to-crosswalk (what the crosswalk claims is "Met" vs. what the cited passages actually say), and guide-to-sources (claims with no pointer, plus one claim whose pointer says something narrower than the guide does).

Two of the findings generalize beyond this document. The first is that *paired documents describing one rule need a single source of truth*: an access matrix in a staff-facing guide and a plain-language disclosure in an athlete-facing appendix are two renderings of the same policy, and maintaining them as independent prose guarantees eventual divergence — here one says "flags only" and the other says the data is visible. The second is attribution precision: Guide §1.4 assigned "unchallengeable, autonomous authority" to Athletic Medicine generally, where the SSI source (`SOURCES.md:63`) assigns it specifically to *primary healthcare providers*. The remedy recorded is not to drop the claim but to restate it with the source's actual subject while keeping Baylor's own Athletic Medicine routing — a correction of who the authority attaches to, not of whether it exists. Three further claims (a seven-unit figure, a nine-retirement figure, and a transfer-history assertion, at guide lines 91–98, 295–301, and 330–334) have no source pointers and were flagged for sourcing rather than removal.

The remaining output was a set of five prose fixes located by line in the generator rather than in the PDF — `scripts/build_guide.py` lines 98, 108, 160, 218, 358 — including a substantive numerical correction ("A voting seat" → "Two voting seats") sitting alongside four stylistic cuts. Because the document is generated, the edit surface is the build script; the PDF is only evidence. This is the same asymmetry that made PyMuPDF inspection the right verification move and `build_guide.py` the right remediation target.

# Compliance Crosswalk "Met" Statuses Overstate Coverage

A compliance crosswalk maps each external recommendation to the passage of a local document that satisfies it, with a status column such as "Met." The 2026-10-04 verification of the Baylor Performance Technology Best Practices guide found that this status column is itself a claim requiring verification: two rows of the SSI crosswalk were marked Met when the cited passages did not actually discharge the recommendation. Check 3 of the 10-point pass failed on this basis alone.

## Key Points

- **A "Met" cell is a factual assertion about a passage, not a label.** Verifying it means reading the cited passage and asking whether it covers the recommendation — the same discipline applied to any citation.
- **Failure mode one: coverage claimed that the cited text never addresses.** Row F2 claimed international-law coverage, but the passages it pointed at say nothing about international law. The row is not weakly supported; it is unsupported.
- **Failure mode two: verb-strength mismatch.** Row Rec 4.3 states that a multidisciplinary group *decides*, while the guide says it *reviews*. "Reviews" does not satisfy a recommendation requiring a decision authority, so the status is an upgrade of the guide's actual commitment.
- **Structural corroboration exposed the mismatch.** Appendix E, the Working Group instrument, contains no decision field — so even the forms confirm the group reviews rather than decides. A missing field in the operative form is evidence against the crosswalk's stronger reading.
- **Remediation is bidirectional.** The recorded fixes were to *either* correct/qualify the crosswalk rows *or* strengthen the underlying artifacts (add a Working Group decision field to Appendix E) — the choice being whether the document should actually meet the recommendation or should stop claiming to.

## Details

The crosswalk is the artifact most likely to be trusted without being checked, because it exists precisely so that a reader does not have to read the underlying document. Someone asking "does this guide satisfy the SSI recommendations?" reads the status column and stops. That makes the status column a high-leverage place for error: an overstated Met cell converts an open gap into an apparently closed one and removes the only signal that would have prompted further work. The two failure modes found here are worth distinguishing because they have different causes. Claiming coverage the text never addresses (F2) is a mapping error — the wrong passage was cited, or none exists. A verb-strength mismatch (Rec 4.3, *decides* vs *reviews*) is subtler: the right passage is cited and it is on-topic, but the recommendation demands a stronger commitment than the passage makes. This is the same gap between topical adjacency and prescriptive match documented in [[connections/retrieval-score-vs-advisor-grounding]] — relevance is not sufficiency.

The Appendix E observation supplies a cheap cross-check for the second failure mode. If a crosswalk row asserts that some body *decides*, the forms that body uses should contain a decision to record; their absence is independent evidence that the asserted authority does not exist in practice. Reading the operative instrument alongside the policy text therefore localizes the error — the same two-independent-derivations logic used elsewhere in this environment — and it also determines the remedy. Where the stronger claim is what Baylor actually wants, the fix is forward: add the decision field and let the guide and crosswalk both say *decides*. Where it is not, the fix is backward: downgrade the crosswalk row to match what the guide commits to. What is not acceptable is leaving a Met status standing on a passage that does not support it, because that is the configuration in which the gap becomes permanently invisible.

# Paired Documents Need a Single Source of Truth for Shared Rules

When one underlying rule is written out in prose in two places — a staff-facing policy section and an athlete-facing disclosure, for example — the two copies will eventually disagree, and nothing in either document reveals the disagreement. The 2026-10-04 verification of Baylor's Performance Technology Best Practices guide found exactly this: Guide §4.3's access matrix grants Athletic/Applied Performance staff *flags only* on raw wellness data, while Appendix A's athlete disclosure states that Athletic Performance sees wellness check-ins. Both documents were internally coherent, correctly built, and correctly styled; the defect existed only in the relationship between them.

## Key Points

- **Each copy reads as correct in isolation.** No internal check on §4.3 or on Appendix A would flag the conflict. Only a cross-document comparison surfaces it, which means the defect is invisible to any per-file review process.
- **The audience split is what drives the divergence.** The same access rule gets restated in different registers — a precise staff matrix versus plain-language athlete prose — and the register change is where the qualifier ("flags only") gets dropped.
- **The athlete-facing copy is the one with legal and ethical weight.** A disclosure that overstates who sees an athlete's wellness data is a consent defect, not a typo; the drift is asymmetric in consequence even though it is symmetric in form.
- **The same failure recurs at the form level.** Appendix A's general research checkbox silently conflicts with Guide §4.5's requirement of IRB approval *plus* study-specific consent, and Appendix B's N/A column conflicts with the guide's statement that rows 1–6 must all be met. In each case a derived instrument quietly relaxes a rule stated upstream.
- **The structural fix is one authoritative rule with the rest generated or explicitly cross-referenced,** not more careful parallel editing. Where generation is impractical, the derived copy should cite the governing section so a reader can detect drift.

## Details

A rule written twice is a rule with two independent edit histories. Once the authoritative text changes — adding a qualifier, narrowing a scope, tightening a gate — nothing propagates the change to the restatement, and the restatement goes on asserting the older, looser version. This is the same mechanism identified in [[concepts/compression-amplifies-distortion]]: the derived artifact drops precisely the qualifiers that constrained the original claim, and because the derived artifact is the shorter, friendlier, more widely read one, the weakened version is the one that reaches the audience. Here the compression is audience-driven rather than length-driven — translating a matrix into disclosure prose — but the loss is identical: "flags only" is exactly the kind of constraint that does not survive translation.

The verification also showed that forms are derived artifacts of the same kind, and that they fail in a particular direction: they *widen* what the governing text narrowed. A general research-consent checkbox appears to discharge a consent requirement that the guide says requires study-specific consent plus IRB approval, so an athlete who signs it and a staffer who reads it both believe a gate has been satisfied. An N/A option on rows the guide calls mandatory converts a hard gate into a soft one, so a contract can pass review without meeting conditions the policy says are required. In both cases the form is the operative instrument — it is what actually gets filled in and filed — so the form's version of the rule is the one that governs in practice regardless of what the guide says. The remedy recorded for the N/A case is instructive: rather than deleting the N/A column, require a documented and approved exception, which keeps the escape hatch but makes using it visible. That is the general shape of the fix wherever a derived instrument must diverge from its source — make the divergence explicit and auditable instead of silent.

# Baylor Professional Development Request Forms (FAST 2026, Databricks Dallas)

On 2026-10-03 two Baylor professional development request forms were finalized as PDFs on the Desktop — FAST 2026 at Texas A&M (Nov 13, $226.80) and the Databricks Data + AI World Tour in Dallas (Oct 14, $174.40) — together with a cover email to supervisor Erin requesting approval. The session's substantive moves were a content *rollback* (a rewritten "Reason for Attending" field reverted to its original wording and verified by reading the text back out of each PDF) and a routing decision: the email was saved as an unsent Gmail draft rather than sent, because the recipient address was inferred rather than confirmed and the connected mail account is personal, not institutional.

## Key Points

- **Both reason fields were rolled back to the original wording, then verified from the artifact.** FAST's rationale is player-tracking / sport business / human performance analytics tied to the football GPS and PFF work; Databricks' is governed data pipelines and AI apps on a lakehouse with hands-on Lakebase and Genie. Totals were unchanged by the rollback ($226.80 / $174.40). Verification read the text back out of each PDF rather than trusting the edit to have applied.
- **The email was drafted, not sent, on two independent grounds.** `Erin_Boyette@baylor.edu` was *inferred* from Baylor's First_Last pattern — it appears in no Gmail history and no local project note — and the connected Gmail MCP account is the personal `eric.rash11@gmail.com`, so a Baylor approval request likely has to be rebuilt in Outlook from the Baylor address.
- **The email existed only in chat until explicitly saved.** Asked where it was, the answer was that it had never been persisted; it was reproduced and then created as a Gmail draft with both Desktop PDFs attached via `gws` `+send --draft`, and pulled back from Gmail afterward to verify subject, body, and attachments.
- **An internal inconsistency across forms was flagged rather than silently resolved:** both forms state "None to date" for other professional development this fiscal year, which conflicts with an HPForum form listing an event on 6/15/26.
- **The work lives on the Desktop, not in a repo,** so the closeout produced no `STATUS.md` update; the handoff was written to `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-10-02-pd-request-forms.md` instead.

## Details

The rollback is the transferable element. A rewrite of the "Reason for Attending" text was produced, reconsidered, and reverted — and the revert was confirmed by extracting the text from each finished PDF rather than by trusting that the edit had been reapplied correctly. For a form that will be signed and submitted, the PDF is the artifact that matters; checking the generator's intent is not the same as checking the document. The same instinct governed the Gmail draft, which was read back from Gmail after creation to confirm that the subject, body, and both attachments had actually landed. In both cases the verification queried the layer that owns the final state.

The send decision records two distinct blockers that happen to point the same way. One is factual: the recipient address is a pattern-based guess, and sending an approval request to a guessed institutional address is a visible failure. The other is structural: the only mail account the tooling can reach is a personal Gmail, and a Baylor approval email sent from a personal address is the wrong artifact regardless of whether the address resolves. Holding the message as a draft keeps the composed text available while leaving both decisions with the user, who must confirm the address and then either send or rebuild it in Baylor Outlook. The remaining items are all human-executed: sign both PDFs (`...Professional Development Request Form_FAST 2026.pdf`, `...Databricks Dallas 2026.pdf`), register for both events (Databricks requires an application for Oct 14; FAST's priority deadline is Nov 1), and reconcile the "other PD this fiscal year" line if the 6/15/26 Global Human Performance Forum was in fact attended — a correction that would have to propagate to both forms *and* the draft.

# Inspect the Built Artifact Instead of Re-Running the Build

During the 2026-10-04 read-only verification of the Baylor Performance Technology Best Practices guide, the twelve PDF deliverables were examined directly with PyMuPDF rather than regenerated. The reason was that `scripts/build_guide.py` drives Microsoft Word through COM automation, so re-running it would have launched and manipulated Word as a side effect of what was supposed to be a non-mutating audit. The choice preserved the read-only guarantee and also happened to verify the right thing: the PDF is the artifact that will be read, so the PDF is what must be correct.

## Key Points

- **A build can be unsafe to invoke for verification.** A COM-driven build manipulates a live application, touches the filesystem, and may leave orphaned processes or modified files — all unacceptable inside a declared read-only pass.
- **Reading the output verifies the artifact; re-running the build verifies the generator's current intent.** These differ whenever the committed output was produced by an earlier version of the generator, or by hand-touched intermediate steps.
- **PyMuPDF made page-level facts checkable without any build.** The pass confirmed a 9-page guide and five 2-page appendices (A–E), twelve deliverables in total, purely by reading the files.
- **Remediation still targets the generator.** The five prose fixes were located by line in `scripts/build_guide.py` (98, 108, 160, 218, 358), not in the PDFs — verification reads the output, editing writes the source.
- **The split keeps the read-only mandate credible.** Declaring a pass read-only and then invoking a build that opens Word would violate the mandate in exactly the way reviewers are least likely to notice.

## Details

The asymmetry here is worth stating plainly: for a generated document, the *output* is the correct verification surface and the *source* is the correct edit surface. Checking the generator's code tells you what it would produce if run now; checking the PDF tells you what is actually in the file that will be signed, distributed, or submitted. Those answers diverge whenever the committed artifact lags the generator, which is routine in any repo where builds are manual. This is the same logic applied to the PD request forms, where the "Reason for Attending" rollback was confirmed by extracting text back out of each finished PDF rather than by trusting the edit to have applied — the artifact is the thing that matters, and the only layer that can confirm its contents is the artifact itself.

The second consideration is cost and safety of the verification step. A build that compiles text to PDF through a pure library is cheap and side-effect-free, and re-running it is a reasonable way to check reproducibility. A build that drives Word through COM is neither: it opens a GUI application, depends on that application's installed state, and can leave processes or temp files behind. In a read-only audit this converts the verification step itself into a mutation, which is precisely the failure that read-only protocols exist to prevent. Choosing PyMuPDF instead is therefore not merely more convenient — it is what makes "no edits, no commits" true rather than approximately true. The general rule is to pick the lightest tool that can read the artifact directly, reserve build invocation for when reproducibility is itself the question, and never let a verification pass acquire side effects heavier than the thing it is verifying.

# Flush Selective Retention on Non-Working Sessions

The memory-compiler flush stage normally emits `FLUSH_OK` — writing nothing to the daily log — when a session produced no durable knowledge. The 2026-08-05 flush demonstrates a middle case: a session that was explicitly "a data snapshot, not a working session," with no decisions and no lessons, but whose contents were nonetheless preserved because several items carried hard deadlines or closing windows. The flush wrote the items down *and* annotated why, making the retention decision auditable rather than implicit.

## Key Points

- **Two distinct retention criteria.** The default criterion is *knowledge durability* (did this session teach something reusable?). The 2026-08-05 flush applied a second, orthogonal criterion: *time sensitivity* (will this item expire or escalate if not surfaced?). An item can fail the first test and still pass the second.
- **The retention rationale was written into the log itself.** The flush appended an explicit note — "This was a data snapshot, not a working session — no decisions or lessons produced. The action items above are preserved only because several are time-sensitive" — so a downstream reader (or compiler) knows the entry is a deliberate exception, not a misclassification.
- **Non-decision content is labeled as such.** The action items were headed "surfaced for follow-up, not new decisions," preventing the compiler from later mistaking a triage snapshot for a decision record.
- **What qualified as time-sensitive:** a security alert, a counterparty's closing availability window (leave dates), and immediate signature/confirmation actions. Ordinary aging replies were included only as context around these.
- **Cost trade-off:** preserving a snapshot costs a small amount of daily-log volume; discarding one risks dropping a deadline entirely, since the snapshot has no other durable home once the session ends.

## Details

The flush stage sits at a lossy boundary: it reads a session transcript and decides what, if anything, survives into `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Its default posture is aggressive discard, because most session chatter is transient and the daily logs are the compiler's source of truth. But a purely knowledge-oriented filter has a blind spot — operational obligations. A triage snapshot contains no lesson, no decision, and no reusable pattern, so it fails a strict "durable knowledge" test, yet it may be the only artifact in the system holding a 3-day-old security alert or a leave window that closes in three days. Once the session closes and the transcript is archived, that obligation has no other retrieval path.

The 2026-08-05 flush resolved this by widening the retention test rather than relaxing it: the items were kept under an explicitly named second criterion, and the reasoning was recorded inline. This self-documenting exception is the transferable practice. It avoids two failure modes at once — silently dropping deadline-bearing content, and silently inflating the log with snapshots that a future reader would mistake for substantive work. The pattern parallels the triage-vs-execution split seen in the inbox-triage runs themselves: surfacing and categorizing is a distinct act from deciding, and labeling output as one or the other keeps the downstream consumer honest. It also complements the broader principle behind the on-ramp pipeline — keep material retrievable while keeping the standing context lean — by admitting only the subset whose expiry cost justifies the space.

# Gate Forms Need Documented Exception Paths, Not N/A Columns

A gate is a set of conditions that must all be satisfied before something proceeds. The 2026-10-04 verification of Baylor's Performance Technology Best Practices guide found that Appendix B — the contract gate form — permits "N/A" on rows 1–6, which the guide states must all be met. An N/A option on a mandatory row converts a hard gate into a soft one: the form can be completed, filed, and approved without any of the six required conditions actually being satisfied, and nothing in the completed form records that a bypass occurred.

## Key Points

- **N/A on a mandatory row is a silent bypass.** The resulting form looks complete and compliant; there is no artifact distinguishing "condition met" from "condition declared inapplicable."
- **The form governs in practice, not the guide.** Appendix B is what reviewers actually fill in and file, so its permissiveness is the operative rule regardless of what the guide requires.
- **The recorded fix keeps the escape hatch but makes it visible:** require a *documented, approved exception* for N/A on rows 1–6, rather than deleting the N/A option outright.
- **Real processes need exceptions; what they cannot tolerate is undetectable ones.** Removing N/A entirely would push edge cases into informal workarounds outside the form, which is worse than an audited exception.
- **This is one of three instances of the same pattern in the same document.** Appendix A's general research checkbox likewise appears to satisfy Guide §4.5's IRB-plus-study-specific-consent requirement, and Appendix A's disclosure likewise relaxes Guide §4.3's "flags only" access rule.

## Details

The design question is what to do when a mandatory condition genuinely does not apply to a particular case — which will happen, since no six-row checklist anticipates every contract. An N/A column answers it in the cheapest possible way and pays for that with auditability: the completed form carries no trace of the judgment, no identification of who made it, and no reviewable rationale. An exception path answers the same question at slightly higher cost and retains all three. The difference matters most in retrospect: when someone later asks whether a given contract met the gate, the N/A version of the form cannot answer, while the exception version can name who approved the deviation and why. That is the same asymmetry behind recording an explicit hold with an enumerated release condition rather than quietly shipping — an exception written down is a managed risk, an exception not written down is an unknown one.

Appendix B's defect also illustrates why gate audits must read the instrument rather than the policy. The guide's text is unambiguous: rows 1–6 must all be met. Nothing in the guide is wrong, and a check confined to the guide would pass. The gate fails only in the form that implements it, and it fails in the direction forms characteristically fail — widening what the policy narrowed, because the form's author was accommodating real-world use while the policy's author was stating a requirement. Both intentions are reasonable; the combination is a hole. The generalizable check is simple and cheap: for every condition a policy calls mandatory, open the form that records it and confirm the form offers no way to complete it without satisfying the condition, or that any such way is itself gated by a recorded approval.

# AT Utilization Benchmarks Project (Baylor Athletic Training / Kitman)

On 2026-06-09, the AT_Utilization_Benchmarks project was built out following two back-to-back meetings — "EOY Kitman Utilization" (Jun 8) and "Athletic Training — Utilization Metrics Standardization" (Jun 9). The session produced a humanized Metric Dictionary v2 with a rebuildable Word deliverable via `python-docx`, and surfaced a critical constraint: Kitman API access is fully vendor-mediated, requiring a fundamental shift in data strategy from iterative incremental pulls to a single comprehensive, precisely-specified request.

## Key Points

- **Metric Dictionary v1 → v2 (humanizer pass):** removed em-dashes, bold-label scaffolding, and template-rhythm artifacts from v1; v2 reads as a practitioner document rather than a template output. A Word version was built via `python-docx` (`scripts/build_metric_dictionary_docx.py`) with Baylor green headings — pandoc is unavailable in this environment, making the direct Python approach the only scriptable option. The script is rebuildable from source on demand.
- **Kitman API lockout — vendor-mediated only:** no direct API access exists at this contract tier. All data pulls flow through the Kitman vendor, killing iterative request cycles. Strategic implication: design one comprehensive, precise data request rather than requesting incrementally. Every field omitted costs a full vendor-mediation round trip. The access constraint also doubles as contract-renegotiation evidence: 17 months remain on the Kitman contract, and paying license fees while needing vendor mediation for access to one's own data is a concrete negotiating point.
- **One-shot request spec design:** target: all teams, CSV format (not PDF), covering treatment, injury, availability, and roster data. The spec must enumerate every field and filter needed across all downstream use cases before submission — second requests for missed fields represent full round trips in calendar time.
- **Carrie as gatekeeper and alignment partner:** emailing Carrie the Metric Dictionary docx both advances the project (her response gates downstream work) and prompts her to share her own documentation materials. Strategy for incoming docs: alignment pass, not a heavier rulebook — adopt her language where it overlaps the five core metrics, keep genuinely new asks minimal to reduce adoption friction.
- **AGENTS.md + CLAUDE.md pointer shim as default pattern:** the project was configured with `AGENTS.md` as the harness-agnostic source of truth and `CLAUDE.md` as a one-line pointer shim. This was explicitly saved to persistent memory as the user's preferred default for all future projects — part of a broader "agentic OS" portability goal across coding harnesses.
- **Sensitivity rules:** trainer names are anonymized in all outbound documents; athlete medical data in `data/` stays local and is never included in shareable outputs or committed to remote repositories.

## Details

The Kitman API constraint is the most architecturally consequential finding from this session. Unlike the Catapult and Perch integrations — where an API exists but behaves unexpectedly from first assumptions (see [[connections/sports-tech-vendor-integration-friction]]) — Kitman offers no API access at all for this contract tier. This eliminates the typical iterative data-exploration workflow (request, inspect, identify gaps, re-request) and replaces it with a single-shot specification design problem. The analyst must enumerate every field, filter, team scope, and format needed across all downstream use cases before submitting the request, because each follow-up is a vendor-mediated round trip measured in calendar days rather than API response times. The "one comprehensive request" framing also changes the preparation work: understanding the full downstream analytical surface (all teams, all metric types, all data joins needed) is prerequisite to the request, not an output of iterative exploration. The framing of Kitman's vendor mediation as contract-renegotiation evidence is strategically useful — making the case for API access in the next contract cycle is strengthened when the gap between paying fees and needing vendor help to access one's own data is documented concretely.

The `python-docx` deliverable pattern establishes a reusable technique for environments where the standard document-conversion pipeline (pandoc) is unavailable. The `scripts/build_metric_dictionary_docx.py` script takes structured metric definitions and produces a formatted `.docx` with organizational branding, making the deliverable reproducible from source — any update to the underlying metric definitions regenerates the Word file in one command without manual reformatting. Word was chosen over PDF as the primary deliverable format because AT staff and clinical collaborators (including Carrie) are more likely to annotate, forward, and edit a `.docx` than a PDF, and editable format reduces the friction of the alignment pass. The project rests in a clean state pending Carrie's response: `docs/carrie_source/` is reserved for incoming materials as read-only originals; derived versions live in `docs/`. Downstream pipeline development (piloting against real Kitman exports, building per-team utilization reporting, Kitman availability widget) should not begin until the Carrie alignment pass is complete and the data request spec has been submitted and fulfilled.

# Do-Not-Send Gate on Audited Deliverables

A do-not-send gate is an explicit, recorded hold placed on a finished-looking deliverable after an audit finds defects that would mislead its audience. On 2026-09-18 the TOS evidence brief was placed under such a gate: the decision was written into working memory rather than left as conversational context, an enumerated fix list was attached as the release condition, and the hold was propagated to a downstream artifact ("Research in 5 #002 (TOS)", built with PR #8 open) that depended on the same uncorrected numbers.

## Key Points

- **The gate is recorded, not remembered.** The do-not-send decision was written to working memory so it survives session boundaries — a finished-looking artifact is otherwise likely to be sent by default later.
- **The gate carries an explicit release condition.** The hold names exactly what must be fixed (three misquotes, the Poisson argument, the order-of-magnitude figure, the source-count claim, the NCAA source-dating, and the over-strong recommendation language), converting "don't send" from a vague misgiving into a closeable checklist.
- **Holds propagate to dependents.** The Research in 5 #002 deliverable was built and had an open PR but was explicitly marked NOT sent, "gated on the same fixes" — a downstream artifact inherits the defects of the numbers it reuses.
- **Risk tiering replaces a binary verdict.** Rather than pass/fail, the audit graded reliance: high risk for causal/comparative/policy use, moderate for the staff-education one-pagers, lower for the long-form review as a source map. This keeps partially-valid work usable for the purposes it can support.
- **"Built and PR-open" is not "ready."** Completion of the production pipeline is orthogonal to correctness of content; the gate sits between them.

## Details

The failure mode a do-not-send gate guards against is specific: an artifact that is complete, formatted, and visibly finished exerts pressure toward release, and any unrecorded reservation about its content erodes over days until someone forwards it. Writing the hold into working memory makes the reservation durable and makes it the first thing a future session encounters when the artifact resurfaces. Attaching an enumerated fix list serves a second purpose — it defines what would *lift* the gate, so the hold is not an open-ended veto but a tracked state with a known exit. Without that list, holds tend to resolve in one of two bad ways: the artifact is quietly abandoned despite most of it being sound, or it is released after a vague "I think we addressed that."

Propagation is the part most easily missed. The Research in 5 #002 piece was a separate, independently completed deliverable with its own open pull request, and nothing about its own build process indicated a problem — its defects were inherited entirely from reusing the brief's numbers. Any hold on a source document must therefore be traced to every artifact that consumed its figures, which in this case also meant the working review, the full PDF, the briefing note, and the one-pagers. The accompanying reliance tiering is what keeps the gate proportionate: the long-form review remained usable as a source map even while the brief was blocked from distribution, because the audit separated "which claims are unsupported" from "which uses depend on those claims." That separation lets legitimate work continue during remediation instead of discarding the whole artifact set.

# Statistical Inference Audit Checklist for Evidence Briefs

The 2026-09-18 adversarial audit of the TOS evidence brief surfaced a reusable set of inferential error patterns that recur whenever a literature review is turned into practice recommendations. The unifying diagnosis was that sources and study-level numbers were largely correct while the *last inferential step* — from observation to causal, screening, or policy claim — was not. The patterns below function as a checklist for auditing any similar brief.

## Key Points

- **Descriptive → causal/screening drift.** The dominant failure: a correlational or descriptive finding is restated as a reason to screen, intervene, or set policy. Check every recommendation against what its cited study design can actually license.
- **"No significant difference" ≠ equivalence.** A null significance test in a small, non-equivalence-designed trial (the cited tennis study had n=10) establishes only that the study lacked power to detect a difference. It is not a safety finding and cannot exonerate an exposure.
- **Reliability/normative data ≠ screening validity.** Datasets establishing that a measure is consistent (pec minor length, DNF, SME, CKCUEST, UQYBT) say nothing about whether that measure predicts the condition of interest.
- **Same-cohort derivation and testing invalidates a cut-point.** An n=49 threshold derived and then tested in the same cohort, with a relative-risk CI of 1.28–68.49, is not a validated screen; the CI width alone signals near-zero information about effect size.
- **Denominator and magnitude hygiene.** Do not juxtapose incompatible denominators (annual incidence vs. 7-year cumulative prevalence). Recompute rhetorical magnitude claims: "four orders of magnitude" for 8.6% vs. 0.004% is actually ~3.33 (ratio ≈ 2,143).
- **Borrowed population rates cannot be applied and then waived.** Using a general-population incidence for an athlete cohort and then dismissing the implication is incoherent — either use an athlete-specific model or state that the expected rate is unknown.

## Details

Two of the patterns deserve particular attention because they are easy to state backwards. The first is the cluster-plausibility argument. Under a Poisson model with the brief's own assumed 4/100,000/yr incidence, a 35-athlete season gives λ = 0.0014, so P(≥2 cases) ≈ 0.000000979 — meaning the model the brief invoked to reassure actually implies the observed two-case cluster is extraordinary. The brief then compounded this by placing a confidence interval around the *observed* event count and using its width as evidence of plausibility; a CI on observed events characterizes uncertainty in the estimate, not surprisingness under an assumed rate, so it answers a different question than the one posed. When a reassurance argument is constructed post hoc, it is worth checking whether the model actually supports the reassurance or contradicts it.

The second is the use of a study design outside the inferential range it supports. A cross-sectional biopsy taken *after* disease onset cannot establish what did or did not cause the disease, yet it was used to exonerate the weight room as a contributing exposure — a temporality violation that no amount of sample size fixes. The same class of error underlies the reliability-as-validity mistake: the studies are real and well-conducted, but they answer "is this measurement repeatable?" rather than "does this measurement predict TOS?", and only the latter licenses a screen. The practical audit procedure that surfaced all of these is a claim-by-claim verification table: for each assertion in the document, record the source, the number as stated in the source, the number as stated in the brief, and — critically — whether the study design supports the inferential use being made. Most rows will pass the first three columns; the fourth is where the findings cluster.

# Code Complete Is Not Verified: Honest Status on Unrun Work

On 2026-10-02 the direct question "Are all the mods complete?" was answered no, despite every mod having been written, passed through the plugin validator, and pushed as commit `7313dcd`. The reason given was that none had actually run. The same session's other two threads produced the complementary cases: a Volleyball_GRID fix whose test was deliberately designed so it *could* fail, and a 42Analytics ingest whose entries had been promoted on the strength of three review rounds that had not caught two-thirds of their defects.

## Key Points

- **Written + validated + pushed is a weaker claim than run.** A validator confirms shape; only execution confirms behavior. Reporting the stronger claim is the error, and the easy affirmative was available and declined.
- **The honest report enumerates the untested surface rather than summarizing confidence.** The dev-mods handoff named specifically what remained unexercised: the Closeout and Closeout+exit buttons, the next-steps buttons, a real `merge-cleanup` branch deletion, `job-watch` coexistence with `statusline-command.py`, and tests that exist but have never executed.
- **A test must be able to fail.** The firewall fix was run with privacy checks *on* and with a baseline that reproduced the original error, after first ruling out a global "always ignore" setting that would have made every test pass vacuously.
- **Residual gaps are stated, not inferred away.** The firewall fix had still never run on Mike Wenger's actual laptop; the closest proxy (both hardcoded usernames deliberately broken, passing at ~7,384 rows) was reported as a proxy rather than as the thing itself.
- **Review rounds are not verification unless they can find the defect.** Three Claude passes left ~65% of the 42Analytics entries defective, which was discovered only by a pass mandated to falsify.

## Details

The three threads on 2026-10-02 form a natural progression of the same principle at increasing cost. In the cheapest case, the gap between "written" and "working" was simply declared, and the cost was a verification checklist handed back with a new-terminal instruction. In the middle case, the gap was closed properly: the test design question "would this test have caught the bug?" was answered affirmatively by constructing a failing baseline, and the orthogonal question "could this test pass for the wrong reason?" was answered by checking the global Excel privacy option before trusting any result. In the most expensive case, the gap had already been crossed — entries were promoted to the vault on the strength of review rounds that turned out not to be verification — so the remedy became a two-location retraction plus relabeling a memory thread whose "PROMOTED" marker now misreported the state.

What ties these together is that each failure of status honesty converts a known gap into an unknown one. An enumerated untested surface stays actionable: someone can run the Closeout button and find out. A claim of completeness removes the prompt to check, which is why a confident false claim is strictly worse than an admitted gap — nothing downstream re-tests it. The same asymmetry explains why a vacuously passing test is worse than no test: it manufactures the appearance of a closed loop. The practical moves the session establishes are therefore three: say "written but not run" when that is the state; design the test so a failing baseline exists before trusting a pass; and when a gate ran too late, treat relabeling the stale status as part of the fix rather than as bookkeeping.

# Claude Code Worktree Gotchas: Branch Orphan, CRLF Normalization, and Windows MAX_PATH

Three non-obvious gotchas around Claude Code's worktree workflow have been documented across sessions. On 2026-05-22, `ExitWorktree` with the `remove` flag deletes the associated branch along with the worktree directory (orphaning any unmerged commits), and Windows `autocrlf` normalization can make files appear different in the working tree even when they are byte-identical inside the Git object store. On 2026-06-17, a third class of failure emerged: Windows MAX_PATH limits on deeply-nested long-filename directories (e.g., PDF libraries in `SourcePapers/`) silently break `git worktree add` / `EnterWorktree`, requiring a sparse-checkout workaround or outright disabling of background-isolation enforcement in `.claude/settings.json`. Additionally, CRLF phantom diffs that accumulate after branch operations can be cleared with `git update-index --refresh` without touching working-tree file content.

## Key Points

- **`ExitWorktree remove` deletes the branch:** the `remove` option on `ExitWorktree` removes both the worktree filesystem and its associated branch in a single operation. Any commits made on that branch that have not been merged or cherry-picked are orphaned — they still exist in the object store but have no branch reference pointing to them.
- **Recovery via `git reflog` + `git cherry-pick`:** `git reflog` records all HEAD and branch-tip movements, including the branch deletion; search for the commit SHA immediately before the deletion event, then `git cherry-pick <sha>` onto the intended target branch. No need to recreate the deleted branch.
- **CRLF vs. LF on Windows `autocrlf`:** Windows Git defaults `core.autocrlf = true`, converting LF → CRLF on checkout and CRLF → LF on commit. Two files can therefore show as "different" in `git status`, shell `==` comparisons, or diff tools because one is CRLF in the working tree while the stored blob is LF — even though they are byte-for-byte identical inside Git.
- **Resolution for CRLF phantom diffs (`git update-index --refresh`):** CRLF-normalized files frequently show as phantom modified in `git status` after branch switches or IDE restarts. Running `git update-index --refresh` resets Git's internal index to match the current working-tree state under the active `autocrlf` policy, clearing false-positive "modified" flags without touching file content. Confirmed on 2026-06-17 to resolve accumulated CRLF index noise in FaceComps after a branch operation.
- **Worktree artifacts should be gitignored:** add `.claude/worktrees/` to `.gitignore` to prevent ephemeral worktree directories from appearing as untracked changes.
- **Windows MAX_PATH breaks worktree creation with deeply-nested long-filename dirs:** repos containing directories with deeply-nested files whose paths exceed 260 characters (e.g., a `SourcePapers/` folder with long PDF filenames) cause `git worktree add` and `EnterWorktree` to fail at the path-length limit. This failure is structural and unrelated to the content of the change being worked on.
- **Sparse-checkout workaround:** create the worktree with `--no-checkout`, then configure a sparse-checkout pattern that excludes the problematic directory (`SourcePapers/`) before checking out. This allows the worktree to be created and populated without ever materializing the long-path files on disk.
- **`.claude/settings.json` to disable background-isolation enforcement:** when worktree creation is structurally broken and sparse-checkout is impractical, adding `.claude/settings.json` with `{"backgroundIsolation": false}` to the repo prevents Claude Code from attempting worktree creation for background agents. The Write tool gate may block direct creation of this file; PowerShell shell mutations are not subject to the same guard and serve as a fallback.

## Details

The `ExitWorktree remove` behavior is easy to trigger accidentally because `remove` reads as a natural cleanup action after agent work in a worktree is done — the intent is "clean up the worktree," but the actual effect includes silently deleting the branch. If the agent made commits during the worktree session that were not merged or pushed, those commits become unreachable by branch name. Git's garbage collector typically does not collect unreachable objects for at least 30 days, so the commits are not immediately destroyed, but they are invisible to normal `git log` traversal and branch listings. The `git reflog` recovery path works because reflog records all reference updates including branch deletions: `git reflog | grep <branch-name>` (or a timestamp search) reveals the pre-deletion commit SHA, and `git cherry-pick` transfers those commits to the current branch without needing to recreate the deleted branch. Prevention: run `git status` and `git log` from inside the worktree before calling `ExitWorktree remove` to confirm all desired commits have been merged or pushed.

The CRLF/autocrlf normalization issue is a Windows-specific environment hazard that has nothing to do with actual file content — two files can fail a shell equality check (`==`) or appear as changed in `git status` while being semantically and functionally identical. This surfaces most sharply in repo-maintenance scripts that compare files byte-for-byte, such as the pre-commit hook described in [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] that checks `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` for divergence. The diagnostic is to inspect raw bytes via `xxd`, PowerShell `Format-Hex`, or `cat -A` rather than trusting diff output or shell comparisons that operate on the working-tree representation. The most reliable cross-platform comparison for script use is `git hash-object <file>`, which hashes the stored blob (always LF after autocrlf normalization on commit) rather than the working-tree bytes. When phantom diffs accumulate after a branch switch or index-state mismatch, `git update-index --refresh` is the non-destructive resolution: it re-reads each tracked file's working-tree state, applies the current `autocrlf` policy to determine what the blob hash should be, and clears any "dirty" flags for files whose content has not actually changed relative to the last commit. On 2026-06-17, this command resolved CRLF index noise in the FaceComps repository after branch operations, with `git status` returning clean immediately afterward without any file modifications.

The Windows MAX_PATH limit failure is structurally different from the previous two gotchas because it is triggered by pre-existing repo content rather than by user actions during the worktree session. Repositories that contain legacy binary archives, PDF libraries (`SourcePapers/`), or deeply-nested generated output directories can accumulate file paths that exceed 260 characters. When `git worktree add` attempts to create a checkout in a new directory, it must materialize all tracked paths within the new worktree's root — any path that would exceed MAX_PATH causes the operation to fail. The sparse-checkout approach resolves this by instructing git to materialize only a subset of the tracked file tree, explicitly excluding the long-path directory from the worktree's scope. The change being made in the worktree (e.g., a UI component update in `src/`) does not require the `SourcePapers/` PDFs to be present, making sparse exclusion both safe and correct. If even sparse-checkout setup is too cumbersome for a given task, disabling background-isolation enforcement in `.claude/settings.json` prevents worktree creation altogether, reverting to inline execution on the main branch — appropriate when the change is demonstrably safe to make without isolation.

# Inbox Triage Methodology (Structured 6-Category Audit)

A structured inbox triage is an ad-hoc deep-audit process that produces a comprehensive categorized snapshot of all pending communications in an email client. Unlike the automated morning email briefing (see [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]]), which delivers a pre-processed summary at a fixed daily time, the inbox triage is run on demand — typically when the communication queue has grown large or when a full reset of communication state is needed. On 2026-06-08, a full audit of Eric Rash's Outlook inbox at Baylor Athletics produced a structured JSON of 50 categorized items across 6 buckets, establishing a prioritized reply and follow-up plan for the session.

## Key Points

- **6-category taxonomy:** `needs_reply` (11), `follow_ups` (3), `meetings_to_schedule` (3), `forms_owed` (3), `still_open` (6), `FYI/newsletters` (24). This taxonomy mirrors the 6-section structure of [[concepts/morning-email-briefing-design]], making triage output directly consumable by the automated morning briefing pipeline and the [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] must-do generator.
- **Structured JSON audit:** the triage produces a machine-readable structured output categorizing all pending items before any replies are written, enabling systematic prioritization across the full queue rather than time-boxing around the first items encountered.
- **Prioritization heuristic: age × importance.** Overdue compliance items (timecards, hard-deadline forms) rank first; then aged replies sorted oldest-first; then newer but high-urgency items. The 2026-06-08 audit surfaced a 9-day-overdue Playfly LLC timecard verification as the single highest-urgency item.
- **FYI/newsletters dominate inbox volume:** 24 of 50 items (48%) required no action. Segregating these into a dedicated FYI category is essential to keeping actionable items visible and preventing low-urgency volume from masking real obligations.
- **Communication debt compounds with age:** 11–13 day stale items (Quin Sandler check-in 11 days stale, Kyle Van Pelt collaboration thread 13 days stale) represent accumulated relational risk; the age-based sort within categories surfaces these items explicitly before newer but less urgent ones.

## Details

The structured inbox triage serves a different function than daily briefings or on-ramp automation. A morning briefing is a push-based system delivering a pre-processed communication summary each day; the inbox triage is a pull-based reset that generates a complete ground-truth snapshot of the full communication queue at a single point in time. The triage is most valuable when the queue has gone unmanaged for several days and the true scope of outstanding obligations is unclear. By producing a structured JSON audit before any responses are written, the triage makes the full scope visible simultaneously — enabling optimal prioritization across the entire queue rather than reactive processing of items in arrival order.

The 2026-06-08 triage revealed a characteristic distribution: FYI/newsletters (48%) were the largest single category by volume but required no action; `needs_reply` (11 items, 22%) was the most operationally important actionable category; and the three remaining actionable categories (`follow_ups`, `meetings_to_schedule`, `forms_owed`) each contained 3 items. This distribution validates the morning email briefing system's 6-section design hypothesis — that most inbox volume is low-urgency FYI, while high-urgency obligations are concentrated in a smaller set of actionable items. The Playfly LLC timecard (9 days overdue) exemplifies the `forms_owed` category's compliance-critical character: unlike email replies where a delay primarily affects relationships, an overdue timecard carries institutional consequences that escalate with each passing day. Age-based prioritization within each category makes these escalating risks visible immediately rather than requiring manual scanning for overdue items.

- [[connections/inbox-triage-and-morning-briefing-taxonomy]] — The cross-cutting connection documenting how the same 6-category taxonomy spans this manual audit tool, the automated morning briefing, and the on-ramp distillation pipeline as a shared architectural contract.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page.
