# NCAA Best Practices Doc: Draft v1 Read-Only Verification

On 2026-10-04 Draft v1 of Baylor Athletics' "Performance Technology Best Practices" guide (repo `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc`, commit `a9dabb0`) was verified read-only against its own `docs/GOAL_PROMPT.md` and `docs/PLAN.md`. The pass ran through Codex with no edits and no commits, applied a 10-point check list, and returned a split verdict: **PASS on checks 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9; FAIL on 3 (SSI crosswalk), 6 (internal consistency), and 8 (factual support)**. All 12 deliverables existed and rendered correctly — a 9-page guide plus five 2-page appendices (A–E). A second read-only round the same evening (R2, HEAD `555702d`) adjudicated a third-party audit of that first review and resolved most findings into specific policy decisions.

## Key Points

- **The artifacts were inspected, not regenerated.** PDFs were read with PyMuPDF rather than re-running the build, because `scripts/build_guide.py` drives Word through COM; re-running it would have produced Word-automation side effects during what was meant to be a non-mutating audit.
- **The three failures are all cross-document failures, not formatting ones.** Build artifacts, outline coverage, pending tags, athlete-data hygiene, terminology, and BaylorDoc styling all passed. What failed was agreement between the guide and its appendices, the accuracy of the SSI crosswalk's coverage claims, and whether specific factual assertions had any source pointer at all.
- **Paired athlete-facing and policy documents drifted apart on the same rule.** Guide §4.3's staff access matrix grants Athletic/Applied Performance *flags only* on raw wellness data, while Appendix A's athlete-facing disclosure says Athletic Performance sees wellness check-ins. R2 settled this: Athletic Medicine sees raw wellness responses; Athletic Performance and coaches see flags only.
- **A consent checkbox silently defeats a stated gate.** Appendix A carries a general research checkbox; Guide §4.5 requires IRB approval *plus* study-specific consent. Signing the general box appears to satisfy a requirement it does not satisfy.
- **A gate form with an "N/A" option is not a gate.** Appendix B permits N/A on rows 1–6, which the guide states must all be met. R2 resolved this as a tiered rule: OGC approval retained for rows 1–3, with rows 4–6 requiring a recorded reason plus Procurement/OGC review (`forms.py:103`).
- **Crosswalk "Met" statuses overstated coverage in two rows.** F2 claims international-law coverage that the cited passages never address, and Rec 4.3 says a multidisciplinary group *decides* while the guide says it *reviews* — with Appendix E providing no Working Group decision field to support the stronger verb. R2's answer: keep a documented Level 3 group decision with delegated Level 2 decisions between meetings, subject to ratification, since recommendation-only fails SSI 4.3's wording (`SOURCES.md:68`).
- **The dominant defect class, named in R2, is proposed framework language presented as current practice.** "Procurement already requires…" described a role the August framework draft only *assigns*; ITS's Aug 13 endorsement covered data-category declaration and standardized intake but not the later routing sheet; a VALD transfer was described as completed when the emails support only an intended workflow; "no record of what happened" to nine retired products overstated an inventory that only asked staff to confirm retention; and a categorical "never in code repositories" claim contradicts live exceptions recorded at `OPEN_ITEMS.md:59–66`.

## Details

The useful structure of the first verification is that every passing check was intrinsic to a single document and every failing check was relational. A pending-tag sweep, a styling check, a terminology check, and an athlete-data hygiene check can each be answered by reading one file. Internal consistency, crosswalk accuracy, and factual support cannot: they require holding two artifacts side by side and asking whether the second is entitled to what it says about the first. This is why a guide can be complete, correctly built, correctly styled, free of placeholder markers, and still be unsafe to publish — the defects live in the seams. The specific seams here were guide-to-appendix (access matrix vs. disclosure; mandatory rows vs. N/A column), guide-to-crosswalk (what the crosswalk claims is "Met" vs. what the cited passages actually say), and guide-to-sources (claims with no pointer, plus one claim whose pointer says something narrower than the guide does).

Two of the findings generalize beyond this document. The first is that *paired documents describing one rule need a single source of truth*: an access matrix in a staff-facing guide and a plain-language disclosure in an athlete-facing appendix are two renderings of the same policy, and maintaining them as independent prose guarantees eventual divergence. The second is attribution precision: Guide §1.4 assigned "unchallengeable, autonomous authority" to Athletic Medicine generally, where the SSI source (`SOURCES.md:63`) assigns it specifically to *primary healthcare providers*. The remedy recorded is not to drop the claim but to restate it with the source's actual subject while keeping Baylor's own Athletic Medicine routing. Three further claims (a seven-unit figure, a nine-retirement figure, and a transfer-history assertion, at guide lines 91–98, 295–301, and 330–334) have no source pointers and were flagged for sourcing rather than removal.

The R2 round added a different kind of value: it adjudicated a prior review rather than re-reading the document from scratch, issuing AGREE / DISAGREE / AGREE-WITH-CHANGE verdicts with `file:line` evidence from `build_guide.py`, `forms.py`, and the `docs/` context files. Three of its outcomes are worth isolating. It answered open factual questions by going to the primary evidence — the `_STALLED\2026-03-09_VALD_Release\` email folder showed only an intended two-school transfer workflow plus a leadership per-sport approval condition, with no completed transfer and no signed releases, and no local Catapult/VALD/Kinexon contract terms establish that individual exclusion from norm pooling is even available. That second finding converted an unconditional individual opt-in into an institution-level prohibition plus athlete notice, pending vendor confirmation (`forms.py:60`) — a vendor-capability-unverified posture rather than a promise the vendor may not be able to honor. It also *rejected* a suggestion: trimming Section 6 was declined because page count alone is not grounds to delete a risk explanation, with the correct next step being to check pagination in the revised PDF first. Finally it surfaced two findings the first pass missed — the framework routing sheet already routes GPS, load monitoring, and force plates to Level 3, so the guide's level table contradicts its own source document; and the Data Steward holds several unique duties with no named backup, a single-point-of-failure gap. The remaining output was a consolidated 5-item fix list spanning `build_guide.py`, `forms.py`, `SSI_CROSSWALK.md`, and `OPEN_ITEMS.md`, plus three external dependencies: an OGC question about CUBI and the Texas Medical Records Privacy Act, vendor questions about norm-pooling exclusion, and confirmation of ITS's position on the routing sheet, which remains unapproved.

- [[concepts/codex-falsify-review-42analytics-ingest]] — The sibling Codex adversarial review: review-only mandate, enumerated checks, and a verdict that enumerates fixes rather than applying them.
- [[concepts/proposed-framework-stated-as-current-practice]] — The defect class R2 named as recurring across this draft.
- [[concepts/review-of-a-review-adjudication-round]] — The R2 adjudication layer that resolved findings into decisions and overturned two of them.
- [[concepts/statistical-inference-audit-checklist]] — The claim-level audit patterns behind check 8; unsourced figures and borrowed authority are the same class of defect.
- [[concepts/deliverable-do-not-send-gate]] — What a split verdict obliges: a finished-looking deliverable held behind enumerated release conditions.

# Proposed Framework Language Presented as Current Practice

The 2026-10-04 R2 adjudication of Baylor's "Performance Technology Best Practices" draft identified a single recurring defect class across otherwise unrelated findings: *proposed or future-state framework language written in the present indicative, so that an intention reads as an established fact*. Five instances were documented in one document. The tense is the whole defect — each sentence would be true as a proposal and is false as a description.

## Key Points

- **"Procurement already requires…"** described a responsibility that the August framework draft merely *assigns*. Assigning a role in a draft is not evidence the role is being performed.
- **Endorsement scope was silently widened.** ITS's Aug 13 endorsement covered data-category declaration and standardized intake; it did not cover the later routing sheet, whose ITS approval remains unconfirmed. A past approval was carried forward onto a newer artifact it never saw.
- **An intended workflow was described as a completed one.** The VALD emails in the `_STALLED\2026-03-09_VALD_Release\` folder support only an *intended* two-school transfer workflow plus a leadership per-sport approval condition — no completed transfer and no signed releases.
- **A gap claim overstated what the underlying process asked.** "No record of what happened" to nine retired products misreads an inventory that only asked staff to *confirm retention*; absence of an answer to a question never asked is not absence of a record.
- **A categorical prohibition had live exceptions on file.** "Never in code repositories" is stated absolutely while `OPEN_ITEMS.md:59–66` records existing exceptions.
- **Role assignment ≠ competency or oversight.** A crosswalk that marks a recommendation satisfied because a role was named overclaims on exactly this basis.

## Details

What makes this class hard to catch is that each sentence is individually plausible and locally sourced — there *is* a framework draft, there *was* an ITS endorsement, there *are* VALD emails, there *was* an inventory. The error is never fabrication; it is a one-step strengthening at the boundary between what a document proposes and what the organization does. A draft that assigns a duty becomes a department that "already requires" it. An endorsement of intake becomes an endorsement of routing. A planned data transfer becomes a performed one. Because the underlying evidence exists, a citation check passes while the claim remains false, which places this defect in the same family as a real citation that does not license the framing it is attached to.

The diagnostic that surfaced all five instances was going back to the primary artifact and reading what it actually says and *when* — the framework draft's verb ("assigns"), the endorsement's date and subject matter, the email folder's contents, the inventory's question. The remedy recorded is uniformly qualified wording rather than deletion: say that the framework assigns the role, that ITS endorsed intake and has not yet weighed in on routing, that a two-school transfer workflow is intended subject to per-sport approval, that retention was confirmed for N units and the remainder is unanswered, and that repository storage is prohibited with documented exceptions. The cost of leaving these uncorrected is specific: a policy document that overstates current compliance removes the signal that the work is still to be done, and it does so in the document most likely to be cited later as evidence that it was done. The related trap is treating a named role as discharged oversight — a crosswalk cannot mark a governance recommendation "Met" because someone was assigned to it, since assignment speaks to neither competency nor whether review actually occurs.

# Review-of-a-Review: The R2 Adjudication Round

On 2026-10-04 the NCAA_BestPractices_Doc repo accumulated a three-layer review stack: `docs/reviews/R0_codex.md` (an initial read-only audit of the draft guide), `docs/reviews/R1_fable.md` (a second model's audit *of that audit*), and an R2 round in which Codex adjudicated R1 — issuing an explicit verdict on every R0 item, every R1 finding 1–9, and the Low-severity items. Verdicts were drawn from a fixed three-value vocabulary (AGREE / DISAGREE / AGREE-WITH-CHANGE), each backed by `file:line` evidence from `scripts/build_guide.py`, `scripts/forms.py`, and the `docs/` context files.

## Key Points

- **The output is a verdict per item, not a new finding list.** Adjudication is a different operation from review: its job is to close open claims, so every prior item gets dispositioned rather than only the interesting ones.
- **A three-value vocabulary is what makes the round productive.** AGREE-WITH-CHANGE is the load-bearing option — it accepts that a defect is real while rejecting the proposed remedy, which a binary accept/reject forces into a false choice.
- **DISAGREE must be exercised for the round to mean anything.** The "trim Section 6" suggestion was rejected as written on the stated ground that page count alone does not justify deleting a risk explanation, with the correct next step being to check pagination in the revised PDF first.
- **Open questions were answered from primary evidence, not arbitrated rhetorically.** Three R1 questions were resolved by reading the VALD email folder, searching for local contract terms, and re-reading SSI Rec 4.3's actual verb — producing "intended not completed", "vendor capability unverified", and "*decides*, so a recommendation alone is not Met".
- **An adjudication round can find what both prior rounds missed.** R2 surfaced the routing sheet's existing Level 3 assignment for GPS, load monitoring, and force plates (contradicting the guide's own level table) and the Data Steward's unique duties with no named backup.
- **Reviews are versioned artifacts in the repo.** Keeping R0/R1/R2 as files under `docs/reviews/` is what makes per-item adjudication possible at all.

## Details

The structural reason to add a layer is that a review's findings are themselves claims, and claims can be wrong in both directions. A second reviewer auditing the first will produce some corrections that are right, some that are right about the defect and wrong about the fix, and some that are simply wrong — and without an adjudication step, all three arrive with equal weight and the document owner resolves them by intuition. Forcing a fixed verdict per item converts a pile of opinions into a decision record, and the file:line requirement keeps each verdict falsifiable: "DISAGREE, `forms.py:103` already requires OGC approval on rows 1–3" can be checked, while "I don't think that's right" cannot. The practical payoff on 2026-10-04 was that the round terminated in a consolidated 5-item fix list plus three named external dependencies, rather than in a longer list of contested findings.

Two behaviors distinguish a real adjudication from a rubber stamp. The first is answering questions by inspection rather than by judgment. All three of R1's open questions were empirical — had the VALD transfer happened, do the vendor contracts permit individual norm-pooling exclusion, and does SSI Rec 4.3 require a decision — and each was answered by going to the artifact: the `_STALLED` email folder, a local search for contract terms, and `SOURCES.md:68`. Two of the three answers were negative findings ("no completed transfer, no signed releases"; "no local contract terms establish exclusion"), which are only available to someone who actually looked. The second behavior is reversing the prior round where warranted. Accepting a plausible-sounding suggestion is cheap; rejecting the Section 6 trim required naming the actual decision criterion (does the risk explanation earn its space) and separating it from the proxy that motivated the suggestion (page count), then specifying the measurement that would settle it (pagination in the revised PDF). An adjudication round that never disagrees has added a layer of cost and no information.

# Compliance Crosswalk "Met" Statuses Overstate Coverage

A compliance crosswalk maps each external recommendation to the passage of a local document that satisfies it, with a status column such as "Met." The 2026-10-04 verification of the Baylor Performance Technology Best Practices guide found that this status column is itself a claim requiring verification: two rows of the SSI crosswalk were marked Met when the cited passages did not actually discharge the recommendation. Check 3 of the 10-point pass failed on this basis alone, and the same evening's adjudication round resolved the stronger of the two rows by changing the governance design rather than the label.

## Key Points

- **A "Met" cell is a factual assertion about a passage, not a label.** Verifying it means reading the cited passage and asking whether it covers the recommendation — the same discipline applied to any citation.
- **Failure mode one: coverage claimed that the cited text never addresses.** Row F2 claimed international-law coverage, but the passages it pointed at say nothing about international law. The row is not weakly supported; it is unsupported.
- **Failure mode two: verb-strength mismatch.** Row Rec 4.3 states that a multidisciplinary group *decides*, while the guide says it *reviews*. "Reviews" does not satisfy a recommendation requiring a decision authority, so the status is an upgrade of the guide's actual commitment.
- **Structural corroboration exposed the mismatch.** Appendix E, the Working Group instrument, contains no decision field — so even the forms confirm the group reviews rather than decides. A missing field in the operative form is evidence against the crosswalk's stronger reading.
- **The resolution strengthened the artifact rather than downgrading the claim.** R2 confirmed from `SOURCES.md:68` that SSI 4.3 says *decides*, concluded that a recommendation-only model fails it, and adopted a documented Level 3 group decision with delegated Level 2 decisions between meetings subject to ratification — plus adding the missing Appendix E decision field.
- **Role assignment is not oversight.** A related overclaim pattern marks a recommendation Met because a role was named; naming a responsible party establishes neither competency nor that review occurs.

## Details

The crosswalk is the artifact most likely to be trusted without being checked, because it exists precisely so that a reader does not have to read the underlying document. Someone asking "does this guide satisfy the SSI recommendations?" reads the status column and stops. That makes the status column a high-leverage place for error: an overstated Met cell converts an open gap into an apparently closed one and removes the only signal that would have prompted further work. The two failure modes found here are worth distinguishing because they have different causes. Claiming coverage the text never addresses (F2) is a mapping error — the wrong passage was cited, or none exists. A verb-strength mismatch (Rec 4.3, *decides* vs *reviews*) is subtler: the right passage is cited and it is on-topic, but the recommendation demands a stronger commitment than the passage makes. This is the same gap between topical adjacency and prescriptive match documented in [[connections/retrieval-score-vs-advisor-grounding]] — relevance is not sufficiency.

The Appendix E observation supplies a cheap cross-check for the second failure mode. If a crosswalk row asserts that some body *decides*, the forms that body uses should contain a decision to record; their absence is independent evidence that the asserted authority does not exist in practice. Reading the operative instrument alongside the policy text therefore localizes the error and also determines the remedy: where the stronger claim is what Baylor actually wants, the fix is forward (add the decision field and let the guide and crosswalk both say *decides*); where it is not, the fix is backward (downgrade the row). The 2026-10-04 adjudication took the forward path, and the design it landed on is instructive — a single Level 3 group decision would stall between meeting cycles, so Level 2 decisions are delegated and then ratified at the group level, which preserves the genuine decision authority SSI requires without making every determination wait for a quorum. What is not acceptable in either direction is leaving a Met status standing on a passage that does not support it, because that is the configuration in which the gap becomes permanently invisible.

# Gate Forms Need Documented Exception Paths, Not N/A Columns

A gate is a set of conditions that must all be satisfied before something proceeds. The 2026-10-04 verification of Baylor's Performance Technology Best Practices guide found that Appendix B — the contract gate form — permits "N/A" on rows 1–6, which the guide states must all be met. An N/A option on a mandatory row converts a hard gate into a soft one: the form can be completed, filed, and approved without any of the six required conditions actually being satisfied, and nothing in the completed form records that a bypass occurred. The same evening's adjudication round converted the fix into a tiered rule rather than a uniform one.

## Key Points

- **N/A on a mandatory row is a silent bypass.** The resulting form looks complete and compliant; there is no artifact distinguishing "condition met" from "condition declared inapplicable."
- **The form governs in practice, not the guide.** Appendix B is what reviewers actually fill in and file, so its permissiveness is the operative rule regardless of what the guide requires.
- **The fix keeps the escape hatch but makes it visible:** require a *documented, approved exception* for N/A rather than deleting the N/A option outright.
- **The resolved design is tiered by stake.** R2 retained OGC approval for rows 1–3 and required a recorded reason plus Procurement/OGC review for rows 4–6 (`forms.py:103`) — the hardest rows keep counsel sign-off, the rest keep an auditable reason.
- **Real processes need exceptions; what they cannot tolerate is undetectable ones.** Removing N/A entirely would push edge cases into informal workarounds outside the form, which is worse than an audited exception.
- **This is one of three instances of the same pattern in the same document.** Appendix A's general research checkbox likewise appears to satisfy Guide §4.5's IRB-plus-study-specific-consent requirement, and Appendix A's disclosure likewise relaxes Guide §4.3's "flags only" access rule.

## Details

The design question is what to do when a mandatory condition genuinely does not apply to a particular case — which will happen, since no six-row checklist anticipates every contract. An N/A column answers it in the cheapest possible way and pays for that with auditability: the completed form carries no trace of the judgment, no identification of who made it, and no reviewable rationale. An exception path answers the same question at slightly higher cost and retains all three. The difference matters most in retrospect: when someone later asks whether a given contract met the gate, the N/A version of the form cannot answer, while the exception version can name who approved the deviation and why. That is the same asymmetry behind recording an explicit hold with an enumerated release condition rather than quietly shipping — an exception written down is a managed risk, an exception not written down is an unknown one.

The tiering that R2 settled on is worth isolating as a general move, because a uniform exception requirement has its own failure mode: if every row demands counsel approval, reviewers route around the form entirely. Splitting rows 1–3 (OGC approval retained) from rows 4–6 (recorded reason plus Procurement/OGC review) matches the friction to the stake, which is what keeps the gate used rather than evaded. Appendix B's original defect also illustrates why gate audits must read the instrument rather than the policy. The guide's text is unambiguous: rows 1–6 must all be met. Nothing in the guide is wrong, and a check confined to the guide would pass. The gate fails only in the form that implements it, and it fails in the direction forms characteristically fail — widening what the policy narrowed, because the form's author was accommodating real-world use while the policy's author was stating a requirement. Both intentions are reasonable; the combination is a hole. The generalizable check is simple and cheap: for every condition a policy calls mandatory, open the form that records it and confirm the form offers no way to complete it without satisfying the condition, or that any such way is itself gated by a recorded approval.

# Do Not Promise What the Vendor Has Not Confirmed It Can Honor

The 2026-10-04 R2 adjudication of Baylor's Performance Technology Best Practices draft replaced an unconditional *individual* opt-in for vendor norm-pooling with an *institution-level* prohibition plus athlete notice (`forms.py:60`). The reason was evidentiary: no Catapult, VALD, or Kinexon contract terms available locally establish that individual exclusion from norm pooling is technically or contractually available, so the form was offering athletes a control no one had confirmed could be enforced. Whether vendors can honor per-athlete exclusion was converted into an explicit open question to ask them.

## Key Points

- **An individual opt-in is a promise of enforcement, not a statement of preference.** Collecting a per-athlete exclusion presumes the downstream system can filter that athlete out of a pooled normative dataset.
- **The capability was unverified, not refused.** No local contract terms establish individual exclusion for Catapult, VALD, or Kinexon; the gap is in what Baylor can confirm, which is a different claim from "the vendors cannot do it."
- **The substitute control is enforceable at the layer Baylor actually owns.** An institution-level prohibition on norm pooling is implemented by Baylor's own contracting and configuration decisions; athlete notice then describes a state of affairs rather than soliciting a request.
- **The unanswered question becomes an action item, not a footnote.** "Ask vendors whether individual norm-pooling exclusion is technically and contractually available" was recorded as a dependency, so the individual opt-in can be reinstated once the capability is confirmed.
- **Consent language is a particularly bad place for optimism.** An unenforceable opt-in is worse than no opt-in: it extracts a signature on a representation the institution cannot keep.

## Details

The structural error being corrected is a mismatch between the layer where a control is offered and the layer where it would have to be enforced. A form in Appendix A sits inside Baylor's own document stack; norm pooling happens inside a vendor's platform, governed by a contract and by whatever filtering the platform supports. Writing an individual exclusion into the Baylor-side form implicitly asserts that the vendor-side system exposes per-athlete exclusion — an assertion the audit could not substantiate from anything on hand. Moving the control up to the institution level relocates it to a layer Baylor demonstrably governs: Baylor can decline norm pooling wholesale as a contracting posture, and it can tell athletes that it has. The guarantee shrinks in granularity and becomes true, which is the correct trade for a consent document.

This is a recognizable instance of the broader vendor-friction pattern across Baylor's sports-tech stack, where a capability's existence has repeatedly turned out to be an assumption rather than a verified fact — Kitman's API access proved vendor-mediated, Perch's auth scheme was the opposite of what was expected, Catapult's token behavior and period aggregation both diverged from documentation. What is new here is the *policy* consequence: when an unverified vendor capability sits underneath an athlete-facing commitment, the appropriate move is not to hedge the prose but to change the commitment to one the institution can satisfy alone, while keeping the stronger version alive as a pending question. The same reasoning kept the VALD two-school transfer workflow described as *intended*, with leadership's per-sport approval condition attached, rather than as completed — in both cases the document was brought down to what the evidence supports, with the gap recorded rather than papered over.

# Connection: Governance Design Must Match the Source's Verb

## The Connection

Three separate defects in the same policy draft were all resolved the same way on 2026-10-04: not by editing the sentence that was wrong, but by changing the governance mechanism underneath it until the sentence became true. A crosswalk row said a group *decides* where the guide said it *reviews* — resolved by creating an actual Level 3 group decision with delegated, ratifiable Level 2 decisions. A gate form permitted N/A on mandatory rows — resolved by a tiered exception path (OGC approval on rows 1–3, recorded reason plus Procurement/OGC review on rows 4–6). A consent form offered individual norm-pooling exclusion — resolved by relocating the control to an institution-level prohibition the institution can actually enforce.

## Key Insight

When a document's language outruns its mechanism, there are always two repairs available: weaken the language, or build the mechanism. The weakening repair is cheaper and almost always wrong when the overstated version is what the organization actually wants — downgrading a crosswalk row to "Partially Met", stamping "N/A permitted" as intentional, or hedging the opt-in with "where available" each leaves the real gap in place while removing the signal that it exists. The strengthening repair is recognizable by a structural test: after the fix, is there a *field, approval, or contracting posture* that would be visibly missing if the claim were false? Appendix E gains a decision field. Appendix B gains a recorded reason and a named approver. The norm-pooling rule gains an institutional prohibition. Each repair leaves a physical trace that can be audited, which is exactly what the original prose lacked.

The verb in the governing source is what sets the bar. SSI Rec 4.3 says *decides* (`SOURCES.md:68`), and that single word is what made a recommendation-only group insufficient and forced the delegation-plus-ratification design. Reading the external standard's verb precisely — decides vs. reviews, requires vs. assigns, must vs. should — is therefore not pedantry but the specification of what has to be built.

## Evidence

- **Crosswalk Rec 4.3:** Appendix E's missing Working Group decision field was independent evidence that the group only reviewed. Fix: adopt a documented Level 3 group decision with delegated Level 2 decisions subject to ratification, and add the decision field — the delegation layer exists specifically so a genuine decision authority does not stall between meeting cycles.
- **Appendix B gate:** N/A on rows 1–6 made a mandatory gate bypassable with no trace. Fix: retain OGC approval for rows 1–3, require a recorded reason plus Procurement/OGC review for rows 4–6 (`forms.py:103`) — friction matched to stake so the form keeps being used.
- **Norm-pooling opt-in:** an individual exclusion presumed an unverified vendor capability. Fix: institution-level prohibition plus athlete notice (`forms.py:60`), with the vendor question recorded as an open dependency so the stronger control can return once confirmed.
- **The contrary case confirms the test.** The suggestion to trim Section 6 was rejected as written because its justification was page count — a proxy with no governance content — and the correct next step was to check pagination in the revised PDF. Not every finding warrants a mechanism change; the ones that do are the ones where a real guarantee is missing.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
